introduction: See no one as an enemy; if someone acts as one, answer with kindness; if kindness makes them worse, be kinder still. The guide repeats this in every form, and gives as its ground that every person is a creature and sign of God. A hundred of its quotations are read here with a hundred from elsewhere. The Sermon on the Mount, which the guide quotes, is the best known; older and wider than it are the proverb about the hungry enemy, the law of the enemy’s ox, Elisha feeding a captured army, Socrates refusing to return evil for evil, Lao Tzu repaying injury with kindness, the Dhammapada’s rule that hatred ceases only by love, and the Qur’an’s that an evil deed repelled by a better one may turn an enemy into a friend. Lincoln, Bacon, Marcus Aurelius, Spinoza and two poets of the battlefield, Hardy and Owen, speak for the same thing. The objections are real. Confucius asks what will be left to repay kindness with; Aristotle calls bearing insult slavish; Machiavelli thinks fear safer than love; the psalmist hates with perfect hatred, and the exiles by Babylon’s rivers cannot sing; Shylock learns revenge from those who wronged him. Paul’s ruler, who must restrain wrong, marks where love of one’s own enemy meets the protection of others.
questions: The guide asks us to see enemies as friends. Is that a change in how one feels, in how one acts, or in what one believes about the other person?
Confucius would repay injury with justice and keep kindness for kindness. What does the guide's teaching ask beyond justice, and what does it risk?
Aristotle calls it slavish to bear insult. How is the forbearance described here different from weakness?
The psalmist hates God's enemies and the exiles in Babylon cannot sing. What should be said to a wronged people who are told to love those who wronged them?
Paul gives the ruler a duty to restrain evil. Where does forgiving one's own enemy end and the protection of others begin?
Several readings say that kindness may make an enemy a friend, and one admits it may make him more bitter. What is the reason for persisting when it does?

outside.why: Jesus gives the same reason: the Father makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good, and sends rain on the just and on the unjust.
Jonah is asked whether God should not spare a great city of people who cannot discern their right hand from their left.
Paul tells his readers not to avenge themselves: vengeance is mine, I will repay, saith the Lord.
Saul weeps and says to David, who has spared him: thou hast rewarded me good, whereas I have rewarded thee evil.
Micah asks only this: to do justly, to love mercy and to walk humbly with thy God.
Jesus tells those he sends among wolves to be wise as serpents and harmless as doves. How are kindness to an enemy and prudence about an enemy to be held together?
In the parable compassion is shown by a Samaritan, one of a people the hearers counted as enemies.
Lincoln told a divided country: we are not enemies, but friends; we must not be enemies.
Leviticus says of the stranger: thou shalt love him as thyself, for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt.
John's Gospel says that greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends.
Spinoza reasons that hatred is increased by being reciprocated, and can be destroyed by love.
Lao Tzu says: to those who are good to me I am good, and to those who are not good to me I am also good.
The Qur'an tells its people to argue with those of other scriptures only in a way that is better.
The law of Moses measured return by injury: eye for eye, tooth for tooth. What did that rule achieve, and what does it leave undone?
Paul tells a mixed church that they are no more strangers and foreigners, but fellowcitizens.
Proverbs says: if thine enemy be hungry, give him bread to eat, and if he be thirsty, give him water to drink.
The Qur'an says that it may be that God will ordain love between you and those with whom you are at enmity.
Asked about repaying injury with kindness, Confucius asks with what, then, kindness will be repaid, and says: recompense injury with justice. Is it just to treat an enemy exactly as a friend?
The Qur'an describes the servants of the Beneficent as those who, when the foolish address them, answer: Peace.
This is the passage: resist not evil, but whosoever shall smite thee on thy right cheek, turn to him the other also.
This is the saying: love your enemies, bless them that curse you, and pray for them which despitefully use you.
Luke gives the same command: love your enemies, do good to them which hate you.
Jesus says that he came not to be ministered unto, but to minister.
Jesus says to those ready to stone: he that is without sin among you, let him first cast a stone.
Acts says that God has made of one blood all nations of men.
Jesus says: blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called the children of God.
On the cross Jesus says: Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do.
The psalmist says of those who hate God: I hate them with perfect hatred, I count them mine enemies. How do people who pray such psalms come to love their enemies for God's sake?
Jesus asks: if ye salute your brethren only, what do ye more than others?
Socrates concludes that we ought not to retaliate or render evil for evil to anyone, whatever evil we may have suffered.
The Qur'an says: repel the evil deed with one which is better, and he who was an enemy will become as a bosom friend.
The Qur'an tells believers not to let hatred of any people seduce them into dealing unjustly.
Paul's instruction is short: bless them which persecute you, bless and curse not.
Aristotle thought that to endure being insulted, and to put up with insult to one's friends, is slavish. Is making no difference between friend and enemy a virtue or a failure of self-respect?
Paul asks that in lowliness of mind each esteem other better than themselves.
Paul says: let us do good unto all men, especially unto them who are of the household of faith.
Peter's letter says: not rendering evil for evil, or railing for railing, but contrariwise blessing.
Jesus speaks of a little leaven hidden in meal until the whole is leavened.
Proverbs says that a soft answer turneth away wrath, but grievous words stir up anger.
Marcus Aurelius says that men exist for the sake of one another: teach them then, or bear with them.
Jesus says to leave the gift at the altar and first be reconciled to thy brother.
Paul says: be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good.
The Dhammapada says that hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love.
The Dhammapada says: let a man overcome anger by love, evil by good, the greedy by liberality, the liar by truth.
Blake found the garden of love filled with graves where flowers should be.
Paul says of himself and his companions: being reviled, we bless; being persecuted, we suffer it.
Lao Tzu says that it is the way of the Tao to recompense injury with kindness.
Jesus says: give, and it shall be given unto you, good measure, pressed down.
Elisha forbids a king to smite his captured enemies, and has bread and water set before them.
Shylock says that if he is wronged he will revenge, by the example he has been shown, and will better the instruction. What is it in the guide's counsel that could break the chain he describes?
Exodus says: if thou meet thine enemy's ox going astray, thou shalt surely bring it back to him.
The Qur'an commands that when ye judge between mankind, ye judge justly.
Jesus says: put up again thy sword, for all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword.
Portia says that the quality of mercy is not strained, and droppeth as the gentle rain from heaven.
Machiavelli advised that it is much safer to be feared than loved. What becomes of love for the tyrant where his advice is followed?
Paul says that he is made all things to all men, that he might by all means save some.
Jesus counts food given to the hungry and welcome given to the stranger as given to himself.
Jeremiah tells exiles to seek the peace of the city where they are captives, and to pray for it.
The psalm says: depart from evil, and do good; seek peace, and pursue it.
Paul says that the ruler is a terror to evil works. How do love for one's own enemies and the protection of others from wrongdoers fit together?
Hebrews says: be not forgetful to entertain strangers, for some have entertained angels unawares.
Proverbs says that a righteous man regardeth the life of his beast.
Proverbs says: rejoice not when thine enemy falleth, and let not thine heart be glad when he stumbleth.
Isaiah foresees swords beaten into plowshares, and nations that learn war no more.
Bacon says that in taking revenge a man is but even with his enemy, but in passing it over he is superior.
Ezekiel hears God say that he has no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn and live.
In the parable the father runs to meet the son who wronged him.
Socrates says that if he must choose, he would rather suffer injustice than do it.
Marcus Aurelius says that the best way of avenging thyself is not to become like the wrong doer.
James asks everyone to be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath.
Peter's letter recalls one who, when he was reviled, reviled not again.
Asked whether to forgive seven times, Jesus answers: until seventy times seven.
Hosea's God keeps drawing with bands of love a people who did not know they were being healed.
A character of Dostoevsky's says that God and the devil are fighting, and the battlefield is the heart of man. When kindness makes another person more bitter, where is the struggle being fought?
Isaiah's servant is oppressed and afflicted, yet he opens not his mouth.
Paul asks that those who oppose be instructed in meekness, by one who is gentle unto all.
Jesus says that if ye forgive not men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive yours.
Paul says that without charity the most eloquent speech is sounding brass or a tinkling cymbal.
Jesus asks why one beholds the mote in a brother's eye and considers not the beam in one's own.
The Song of Solomon says that many waters cannot quench love, neither can the floods drown it.
Whitman says that whoever walks a furlong without sympathy walks to his own funeral.
Stephen, as he is stoned, kneels and cries: Lord, lay not this sin to their charge.
Owen's dead soldier says to the one who killed him: I am the enemy you killed, my friend.
Luke names Mary called Magdalene among the women who followed Jesus and ministered to him.
Hardy's soldier finds war quaint and curious: you shoot a fellow down you'd treat if met where any bar is.
The Qur'an praises those who control their wrath and are forgiving toward mankind.
Joseph says to the brothers who sold him: ye thought evil against me, but God meant it unto good.
Lincoln asked for malice toward none and charity for all at the end of a war.
The exiles by the rivers of Babylon wept and could not sing. What does it cost a wronged people to treat those who wronged them with love and concord?
The Qur'an says that the reward of an ill deed is the like of it, but whoever pardons and amends, his wage is with God.
Prospero, with his enemies in his power, says that the rarer action is in virtue than in vengeance.
Twain's stranger tells a congregation what they have also prayed for when they prayed for victory. What does it take to pray honestly for an enemy?
Augustine says that our hearts are restless until they rest in God.
Jesus says to give without letting the left hand know what the right hand does.
Paul says: if thine enemy hunger, feed him; if he thirst, give him drink.
Paul says: let us not be weary in well doing, for in due season we shall reap.
Tennyson foresaw the war-drum silent and the battle-flags furled in the Parliament of man.
Paul says that faith, hope and charity abide, and the greatest of these is charity.
Jesus says that all men shall know his disciples by their love.
Nietzsche said that blood is the very worst witness to truth. What would a critic who suspects weakness behind forgiveness say to 'recognize your enemies as friends', and what is the answer?

exodus-thine-enemys-ox.text: If thou meet thine enemy's ox or his ass going astray, thou shalt surely bring it back to him again. If thou see the ass of him that hateth thee lying under his burden, and wouldest forbear to help him, thou shalt surely help with him

samuel-thou-hast-rewarded-me-good.text: And it came to pass, when David had made an end of speaking these words unto Saul, that Saul said, Is this thy voice, my son David? And Saul lifted up his voice, and wept. And he said to David, Thou art more righteous than I: for thou hast rewarded me good, whereas I have rewarded thee evil. And thou hast shewed this day how that thou hast dealt well with me: forasmuch as when the Lord had delivered me into thine hand, thou killedst me not. For if a man find his enemy, will he let him go well away? wherefore the Lord reward thee good for that thou hast done unto me this day

kings-set-bread-and-water-before-them.text: And the king of Israel said unto Elisha, when he saw them, My father, shall I smite them? shall I smite them? And he answered, Thou shalt not smite them: wouldest thou smite those whom thou hast taken captive with thy sword and with thy bow? set bread and water before them, that they may eat and drink, and go to their master. And he prepared great provision for them: and when they had eaten and drunk, he sent them away, and they went to their master. So the bands of Syria came no more into the land of Israel

peter-not-rendering-evil-for-evil.text: Not rendering evil for evil, or railing for railing: but contrariwise blessing; knowing that ye are thereunto called, that ye should inherit a blessing

psalm-i-hate-them-with-perfect-hatred.text: Do not I hate them, O Lord, that hate thee? and am not I grieved with those that rise up against thee? I hate them with perfect hatred: I count them mine enemies

quran-whosoever-pardoneth.text: The guerdon of an ill-deed is an ill the like thereof. But whosoever pardoneth and amendeth, his wage is the affair of Allah. Lo! He loveth not wrong-doers.

analects-recompense-injury-with-justice.text: With what then will you recompense kindness?" "Recompense injury with justice, and recompense kindness with kindness
analects-recompense-injury-with-justice.author: Confucius

owen-i-am-the-enemy-you-killed.author: Wilfred Owen
